The insecticides used in veterinary practice are often classified as topical or systemic ectoparasiticides. Top- ical ectoparasiticides are applied topically to the host animal (such as dogs or cats) to kill its ectoparasites (such as fleas). In the case of systemic ectoparasiticides the term ‘systemic’ refers to the ingestion of the insec- ticide by the ectoparasite from the host’s blood; the in- secticide may be present in the host’s blood either as a result of absorption through the skin after topical appli- cation or after systemic dosage. Molluscicides are used in agriculture or horticulture or in the domestic garden to control snail and slug pests. Additionally, molluscicides such as niclosamide (de- scribed in the Anthelmintics chapter on p.151) are used against the freshwater snail vector Bulinus in the con- trol of schistosomiasis. Rodenticides may be used to exterminate rats and mice which may be vectors for diseases such as lepto- spirosis, plague, rat-bite fever, and some haemorrhagic fevers. Many rodenticides are anticoagulants. Warfarin (p.1425) is a commonly used rodenticide. Clinical Uses of Pesticides and Repellents Pediculosis Two species of louse cause pediculosis1-7 in man; these are Pediculus humanus with its two varieties, Pediculus humanus capitis (the head louse) and Pediculus humanus humanus (the body louse), and Pthirus pubis (Phthirus pubis) (the pubic or crab louse). Unlike the head louse, the body louse is an important vector for a number of infec- tions including epidemic typhus (p.198), trench fever (p.196), and relapsing fever (p.189). Insecticides used in the treatment of head lice include the organophosphate malathion, and some pyrethroids such as bioallethrin, permethrin, phenothrin, and tetramethrin. The carbamate, carbaryl, is also effective, although there has been some concern over a theoretical risk of carcinogenic- ity. Lindane has been used but is no longer recommended as a first-line treatment due to its neurotoxicity and resist- ance. To be effective insecticide products need to be ap- plied correctly; a quantity of 50 to 100 mL should be ap- plied thoroughly to the hair from hair root to the tip and left on for 8 to 12 hours.
